By midday the wind picked up and fine grit worked its way into every zipper and seam, so they stopped to tighten the tarps and check the antenna mast. On the second day they mapped a shallow basin where ancient shorelines had left pale terraces along the hillsides, and each member took turns sieving sediment, labeling jars, and photographing strata. A sandstorm on the third afternoon forced them to shelter behind the vehicles for hours, listening to grit hammer the metal panels while the radio crackled with static from the base camp far away. Tempers frayed briefly over a miscounted water ration, but the team leader settled it with an extra rest stop and a shared tin of peaches. By the fourth day they had settled into a steady rhythm: rising before dawn, walking the transect lines while the air stayed cool, logging each soil core with its position tag, and resting at noon beneath the striped awning while the sun bleached the horizon white. After the midday break they calibrated the drone, flew two grid patterns over the eastern dunes, and argued cheerfully about whether a dark streak on the imagery marked an old riverbed or merely a shadow. In the evening they cooked lentils over a hissing burner, compared blister tallies, and plotted the next traverse by lantern light as beetles clicked against the glass.
